aDefectNoCounterCanSee.what: scripts/rcap-packet-completeness/verify-identity-refresh-survives-rebuild.mjs keys every annotation as `path::identityRefresh.was.sha256`. The ONLY correct repair for a pin whose shared record drifted again -- re-do the anchor comparison and write a fresh annotation, which the module's own failure text asks for in as many words -- necessarily moves `was` and therefore changes the key. The tripwire reported both of this lane's correctly re-anchored receipts as 'annotations ERASED BY A REBUILD' and exited 1.
aDefectNoCounterCanSee.whyThatIsWorseThanNoise: the module's own comment explains that a check crying wolf under a common condition teaches its readers to ignore it, and costs more than the defect it was written for. It said that about sparse checkout; it is now true of the repair it exists to protect.
aDefectNoCounterCanSee.repair: a dropped annotation is EXCUSED only when the receipt still carries an annotation AT THE SAME PATH whose `was.sha256` is the identity the dropped annotation ended at -- the chain continues through it, and a human compared anchors across the second move. Nothing else is excused.
aDefectNoCounterCanSee.controlProvingItStillFails: with the annotation deleted outright from the Arkansas receipt, the tripwire still names the file, still says '1 of 1 identityRefresh annotation(s) dropped', and still exits 1. With the annotation restored it exits 0.

aSecondDefectNoCounterCanSee.what: The same pin on data/record-clearing/legal-design-packet-set-manifests.json has now gone stale TWICE in five days -- 563147bf -> 6076f734 (repaired 2026-09-05) -> 80b5e071 (repaired here) -- and no counter reported either. Twelve family source receipts bind that file. VF08 measured 7 of 12 as not binding exact at ITS base; that count is itself stale now, because the file moved three more times.
aSecondDefectNoCounterCanSee.theStructuralPoint: this is not a family defect being fixed twelve times. It is a shared, mutable repository record bound as though it were a source. Re-anchoring is a treadmill: every route-productization commit re-breaks every receipt that pins it, and the verifier reads the receipt's own boolean instead of recomputing, so the fleet reads green the whole time.
aSecondDefectNoCounterCanSee.whatThisLaneDidNotDo: it did not re-anchor the other ten families. That is outside its grant, and doing it family-by-family is the treadmill rather than the fix. VF08's own question is the right one and is above a repair lane: whether a record other lanes rewrite several times a week should be bound by whole-file SHA-256 at all, or bound by the entries a family actually reads.
aSecondDefectNoCounterCanSee.whatIaLaneDidInstead: for ia-12347-set, where this lane authored a new dependency on two shared records, it deliberately bound them by verbatim content assertion rather than whole-file digest, so this failure mode cannot start there.

aThirdThingWorthSaying.what: Two of the four dispatched findings were partly stale and neither was wholly stale, and telling those apart mattered.
aThirdThingWorthSaying.detail: VF06 and VF08 each named a receipt pin (563147bf) that a 2026-09-05 repair had already corrected at a later commit than their declared bases. Reporting them as STALE and stopping would have been wrong: the obligation still fails at this base, on a number neither lane ever saw. Reporting them as plain FAIL without saying so would have hidden that the 2026-09-05 repair happened and worked. Both rows say both things.
